name: Itoshiro no Ōsugi

location.address: Itoshiro, Shirotori-cho, Gujo, Gifu Prefecture, Japan (within Hakusan National Park, on the Mino Zenjo-do pilgrim trail)

access: Free, public. Reached by a maintained hiking path with 420 stone/concrete steps from a parking area near Hakusan Chukyo Shrine, about 300m distance and 90m elevation gain; roughly a 2-hour approach including the drive/bus from Mino-Shirotori. No entry fee or gate. Note: as of 2025 the forest access road to the trailhead has had closures from fallen trees and landslides, restricting general access at times; check current road status before travelling.
transport: Nearest station Mino-Shirotori (Nagaragawa Railway), then bus/drive roughly 50 minutes to Itoshiro, then the 300m/420-step trail on foot.
verify_notes: One of Japan's most famous giant sugi, ranked among the largest cedars in the country by girth (a 2023 visitor blog cites it as roughly 5th largest by girth). Legend: the tree is said to have grown from the walking staff of the priest Taicho, who opened Mt. Hakusan to religious practice; it stands as a landmark on the Mino Zenjo-do, the Hakusan-faith pilgrim trail (ascetic mountain route). Designated a National Natural Monument on 1924-12-09 and upgraded to Special National Natural Monument (Japan's highest tier) on 1957-07-02 -- Gifu Prefecture's only wooden Special Natural Monument. Girth given as 14m by Wikipedia/Wikidata/tourism board and 13.1m by local on-site signage per a 2023 visitor account; recorded girth_cm as 1400, note the signage discrepancy for the writer. Height 24-25m. Age uniformly cited as 'over 1,800 years' by Wikipedia, the prefectural tourism site and Wikidata; no single dated planting record exists (as expected for a tree this old), so treat 1,800 as the repeated estimate rather than a precise figure -- kept the age band broad. CONDITION: multiple sources agree roughly half the trunk has died back while the other half remains healthy and green; a 2023-published blog account of 2017 and 2019 visits describes the living half as warm and clearly alive, not a dead specimen. This is a documented partial dieback, not a dead tree -- passes the 'alive now' bar but the most recent first-hand confirmation found dates to 2019 (blog published 2023), so flagging rather than marking fully current; a 2025 community-hall notice about the annual pilgrim-trail cleanup (organised by Itoshiro residents) shows the site is still actively used/maintained as of this year, which is corroborating but not itself a sighting of the tree. DESTINATION TEST: passes clearly -- Special National Natural Monument status, a purpose-built 420-step staircase exists specifically to bring visitors to this one tree, and it is one of the handful of giant cedars Japanese enthusiasts specifically travel to see (a genre of its own, 'kyoju tanbo' / giant-tree pilgrimage blogs exist just for trees like this one). CONTAINER: Itoshiro is a remote mountain hamlet in Gujo, Gifu; not within a day-trip boundary of any published city. Recommend as its own single-tree place under the 2026-08-31 exception, named 'Itoshiro' or 'Itoshiro, Gujo'.
